## Answer: 39

**Lower bound.** Each player plays exactly one match per round and must face 39 different opponents, so the tournament lasts at least 39 rounds.

**Construction (sketch).** Take the standard 1-factorization of $K_{40}$ on the vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_{39}\cup\{\infty\}$, with factors $F_i=\{\{\infty,i\}\}\cup\{\{i+j,\,i-j\}: j=1,\dots,19\}$ for $i\in\mathbb{Z}_{39}$. Let round $t$ pair players according to $F_t$.

- **Court dynamics.** The pairings of round $t+1$ are determined by the round-$t$ results. Each court sends one player to each of its two neighbours in the cycle $\Gamma$ on courts $1\!-\!3\!-\!5\!-\cdots\!-\!19\!-\!20\!-\!18\!-\!\cdots\!-\!2\!-\!1$, and each court's two players can be routed to its two neighbours in either order by choosing the winner. So any sequence of pairings $M_0,M_1,\dots$ is realisable provided consecutive unions $M_t\cup M_{t+1}$ are Hamiltonian and the cyclic order of the $M_{t+1}$-edges is the same along $M_t\cup M_{t+1}$ and $M_{t+1}\cup M_{t+2}$ (up to reversal).
- **Verification.** For $F_t$ the union $F_t\cup F_{t+1}$ is a Hamiltonian cycle, and the edge orders agree (the two walks alternate $x\mapsto -x$ and $x\mapsto 2-x$, resp. $x\mapsto 4-x$, and one checks the orders are reverses of each other). The condition is invariant under the rotation $F_t\mapsto F_{t+1}$, so it holds for all $t$.
- **Check on small cases.** I verified the same scheme explicitly for 4 players (3 rounds), 6 players (5 rounds) and 8 players (7 rounds), with every pair meeting exactly once.

With $t=0,\dots,38$ the 39 rounds realise all $\binom{40}{2}=780$ pairs exactly once, so 39 rounds suffice.

ANSWER: 39
